הארכיטקטורה בדוח (§8.3)

8.3.1 Transmon lattice — Transmon lattice with tunable couplers (sc)

The idea. A transmon (transmon) is a capacitively shunted Josephson junction whose two lowest levels serve bare as the qubit (enc_bare). The architecture tiles transmons in a lithographic lattice (cx_nn), switches neighbour exchange with flux-tuned couplers (g_tc), drives them from room-temperature racks (ct_rt), reads them dispersively (ro_disp) and corrects with the rotated surface code, whose weight-4 checks are the lattice's own neighbourhoods. A circuit atom is drawn, not found: gates take tens of nanoseconds [G] and the QEC cycle 1.1 µs [D][1], the map's fastest clock (§7.4). The price is coherence (T₁ 68 µs on Willow [D][32]), identical qubits and any coupling beyond the neighbour. The bet: speed and wafer fabrication outrun the error budget; links between chips come later.

What it needs. Everything rests on fab_sc: the transmon requires junction lithography, so its frequency spread is fixed at fabrication; the trimming that repairs it has no technology yet. The surface code requires only neighbour checks. Bivariate-bicycle codes keep 12 logical qubits in 288 physical where the surface code needs nearly 3,000, but need a degree-6 graph [S][248]: code_qldpc requires long-range couplers (cx_lr) and conflicts with cx_nn, open since 2024-03. Readout and reset are two-thirds of the 651 ns derived round [S] (§7.4). Four control technologies replace one another per signal, not per machine — a Heron r2 ran cryo-CMOS flux ASICs in hybrid with room-temperature RF (Mar 2026) [C]. Both cold routes conflict with the transmon: cryo-CMOS (ct_cryocmos) on the mixing chamber's heat budget, SFQ (ct_sfq) on quasiparticles — its switching photons break Cooper pairs, 0.96(2)% of a 1.2(1)% error per Clifford in 2023 [D][249], mitigation projected, not yet independently measured. Encoding has one option; the microwave–optical transducer slot is empty.

Where it stands. 75 of the register's 160 machines and 54 devices (Table 8.3): 35 deployed, 14 demonstrated, 6 retired, 17 announced or planned, 3 other; IBM supplies 19 rows, China 16. The largest gate-capable device remains IBM Quantum Osprey, 433 qubits (2022); Condor's 1,121 never reached users. The best 2Q error, 1.0×10⁻³ on Origin Wukong-180 (4th gen), is a company figure [C] (Table 8.3); Willow's device mean is 99.88% [D][32]. Willow ran d=7 at Λ = 2.14 [D][1], then 7.72×10⁻⁴ per cycle (Jul 2026) [D][2]; Zuchongzhi 3.2 d=7 at Λ = 1.40 [D][3]. Code, decoder and interconnect slots are empty on 59, 67 and 57 machines; 12 rows publish no gate mechanism; 311 of 812 evidence cells are documented.

Exceptions and borrowings. No machine falls off the slots or fits another architecture better; alternates carry the direction. Wiring leaves the chip edge (ct_vio) on RIKEN 64, RIKEN–Fujitsu 256, OQC Toshiko and QuantWare Bass-A10K (VIO-40K), racks still warm; control goes cold only in part or at small scale: cryo-CMOS flux ASICs in hybrid with room-temperature RF on Heron r2 and as alternate on Starling and Blue Jay, SFQ on SEEQC's five-qubit system (single-qubit gates only) and QuamCore (design only). Sycamore and Zuchongzhi stack dies (ic_multidie); modules (ic_mcm) ship only on Rigetti Cepheus, at 99.6%→99.1% [C][36]. IBM's utility line sits in mitigation (code_mitig: Eagle, Heron r3, Nighthawk r2) and detection (code_detect: Falcon, Heron r2/r3, Origin Wukong 3rd gen); qLDPC runs only on Kunlun. Nominal members: Osprey, Eagle, Condor, Falcon and LBNL AQT use cross-resonance (g_cr), not tunable couplers; targets (Amaravati, CSCS, KRISS 50); plans (Kookaburra to Blue Jay, Fujitsu 10,000); component testbeds (Toshiba coupler, Loon); undisclosed stacks (Tianyan-504, RIKEN–Fujitsu 256, Toshiko). Gap cells show the architecture drawn too narrowly: a central-resonator bus (IQM Star 24, VLQ, DRDO–TIFR), leakage-removal units (Willow, Zuchongzhi 3.2), post-fabrication frequency trimming (Willow, Cepheus, Academia Sinica). Dual-rail borrows transmon, ct_vio and ic_mcm; cat ic_multidie; spins ct_cryocmos.

The next test. Expectations to 31 Mar 2028 (§5.2). A bivariate-bicycle memory on c-couplers, Kookaburra or a Kunlun successor, reports a logical error per cycle below its physical idle error; Kunlun's 8.91% [P][72]–[74] is the baseline. If Kookaburra is undelivered again by end-2027, the qLDPC branch is demoted and the architecture stays a surface-code machine at >10³ physical qubits per logical at 10⁻⁶ [S] (§2.1). And a gate-capable device above 433 qubits with published two-qubit errors, plus cryo-CMOS or SFQ control of ≥50 qubits; if neither appears and readout stays near 10⁻², scale by fabrication is demoted to scale by modules.

What the builders say. Google argues that superconducting processors scale in circuit depth, with microsecond cycles, while neutral atoms scale in qubit count [C][2], [9], and expects commercially relevant superconducting machines by the end of this decade, naming no qubit count [R][2], [9]. Rigetti targets about 1,000 qubits at 99.9% two-qubit fidelity in roughly three years, built from chiplets [R][61]. Fujitsu is building a machine of more than 10,000 physical and 250 logical qubits for fiscal 2030 [R][75], [76]. IBM chose a qLDPC code (a low-density parity-check code whose checks join distant qubits) because it corrects as well as the surface code with ten times fewer qubits [D][481]; it plans Kookaburra, the first qLDPC module, for 2026 and Starling, 100 million gates on 200 logical qubits, for 2029 [R][481].
